lens: facts and integrity: every quotation, number, date, name, title and attribution checked against the claims ledger, the ESV copy, the BSB, local primary texts, and 11 web searches

findings.where: ## What Nietzsche Said About George Eliot, third paragraph, first sentence: "The early Christians acted on that belief long before they had any power, as what they did for the children Rome threw away shows."
findings.problem: (c) Mismatch with the ledger and with the site's own sister essay. The published JSON dropped the link to /writing/the-children-rome-threw-away, because that essay is not on the shelf. The ledger had relied on that link ("Detail is left to the linked essay"). Now the clause stands alone. "What they did for the children Rome threw away" reads as the familiar story that early Christians rescued other people's abandoned babies. The ledger's sources support only refusal: Didache 2, Epistle to Diognetus 5 ("they do not destroy their offspring") and Justin, First Apology 27 ("to expose newly-born children is the part of wicked men"). All three were re-read today in scripts/data/history-sources/texts. The sister essay and its ledger (Livewell-/docs/work/essays/ledgers/the-children-rome-threw-away.md, lines 58 to 63) say this rescue story "runs ahead of the evidence". They say evidence of Christians taking in other people's foundlings comes later: Augustine in 408 and the Council of Vaison in 442, both after Constantine. So the sentence claims something the platform itself has found unsupported for the period before Christians held power.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "The early Christians acted on that belief long before they had any power. Where abandoning an unwanted newborn was common and accepted, they refused to abandon their own, and Justin told the emperor so." Leave the next sentence ("The secular person who takes the equal dignity...") as it is. In the ledger line on Rome and the newborn, delete "Detail is left to the linked essay" and cite Justin, First Apology 27, as the source for "told the emperor so".

findings.where: ## Moral Facts Without God, last paragraph, second sentence: "He can follow Wielenberg in holding that moral facts are simply there, necessary and unexplained, and still owe Street an answer about how creatures shaped by selection came to know them."
findings.problem: (f) Living person. "Still owe Street an answer" reads as if Wielenberg's view has no reply to Street. Wielenberg has published one: the "third factor" account, developed in Robust Ethics (2014), in which our cognitive faculties account for both the moral properties and our beliefs about them. The ledger itself records this ("fair to Wielenberg, who does offer a reply") and still left the sentence as written. A search today again found the reply reported, though only in secondary summaries: moralapologetics.com "Wielenberg on Evolutionary Debunking Arguments", the philpapers record DYKBBT (a critic arguing that third-factor replies fail), and the Washington and Lee Mudd Center journal. A reader who knows the literature would find the sentence unfair to him.
findings.fix: Replace with: "He can follow Wielenberg in holding that moral facts are simply there, necessary and unexplained, and then has to answer Street's question about how creatures shaped by selection came to know them. Wielenberg has offered an answer, and the argument over it goes on." Add the third-factor reply and its sources to the ledger line for this sentence.

findings.where: Second paragraph, last sentence: "Myers wrote that perhaps no voice had ever affirmed more sternly the rule of a law that was impersonal and promised no reward."
findings.problem: (g) Restoration. The ledger records the writer's original quoted fragment, "the sovereignty of impersonal and unrecompensing Law". It was kept out because the printed copies disagree. Today I re-read Morley (PG 17954, local) at the passage. It prints "Never, perhaps, had sterner accents affirmed the sovereignty of impersonal and unrecompensing law." The restoration pass's search result quoting Wikiquote, which cites the Century Magazine of November 1881, also has "unrecompensing", as does the online-literature.com forum transcription. Only Cooke (PG 11680, re-read today) has "unrecompensed". Three copies agree on the two words "impersonal and unrecompensing". What stays unsettled is "had" against "have" and the capital on "Law". Two searches today did not find the 1881 Century text or Myers's Essays: Modern (1885). Quoting only the two words avoids both doubts and gives back Myers's own adjective, which the essay's ending answers ("the law she served was not impersonal after all").
findings.fix: Replace with: Myers wrote that perhaps no voice had ever affirmed more sternly the sovereignty of a law that was, in his words, "impersonal and unrecompensing." Do not quote more of the sentence, and do not capitalize "Law", unless the 1881 Century printing is seen. If the fixer wants zero residual risk, keeping the current paraphrase is also acceptable.

findings.where: ## When Christians Were Called Atheists, Bayle paragraph, first sentence: "...and a Protestant minister there later attacked him for it until he lost his professorship."
findings.problem: (c) The ledger's sources disagree about why Bayle lost his chair, and "for it ... until" picks one of them. Robertson ties the 1693 deprivation to the freethinking of the Pensées sur la comète. EB1911 "Bayle" (cited in the ledger) puts the quarrel down to envy and to the Avis aux réfugiés (1690). Britannica, as a search summary today showed it, says Bayle's plea for toleration, extended even to atheists, convinced Jurieu he was "an atheist in disguise", and that the 1693 loss followed the break over Bayle's conciliatory stance toward Louis XIV. The minister attacking Bayle and Bayle losing the chair are both solid. That the comet argument alone caused the loss is not.
findings.fix: Replace the clause with: "and a Protestant minister there came to think him an atheist in disguise and attacked him until he lost his professorship." Add the Britannica summary to the ledger line alongside Robertson and EB1911.

findings.where: ## What Nietzsche Said About George Eliot, first paragraph, second sentence: "Sixteen years after that evening in Cambridge, he published Twilight of the Idols"
findings.problem: (c) The ledger's arithmetic counts calendar years (1873 to 1889). Its own source, Ludovici's preface, says the book "first appeared at the end of January 1889". From May 1873 that is fifteen years and eight months, so "sixteen years after that evening" is slightly over.
findings.fix: Replace "Sixteen years after that evening in Cambridge" with "Not quite sixteen years after that evening in Cambridge".

findings.where: ## What Nietzsche Said About George Eliot, fourth paragraph: "...and in churches that protected their own reputation at the expense of the people they had harmed."
findings.problem: (a) This claim has no ledger line. The ledger covers only the slavery half of the sentence. The claim is general, names no church, and is well documented, so the text can stand.
findings.fix: No change to the essay text. Add a ledger line citing a public record the fixer verifies before recording it, for example the May 2022 Guidepost Solutions report to the Southern Baptist Convention or the 2018 Pennsylvania grand jury report. Keep the essay itself unnamed, as written, so it does not imply James's denominational ties.

clean_checks: Scripture (e): I compared all 13 quotations to the ESV copy (lguenth/mdbible fd66568), punctuation included. Romans 2:14-15, James 1:17, Genesis 9:6, Romans 2:1, 2:21, 2:24 and 3:23, Mark 10:17, 10:18, 10:21 and 10:27, and the closing Mark 10:18, Romans 2:15 and Luke 19:10 all match in words. The one punctuation difference is James 1:17: the copy drops the comma after 'Father of lights', and the final pass's search of esv.org and biblia.com shows the comma the essay has. Every quotation carries its reference, and each reference matches the verse's sense in the BSB (client/public/bible/ch). The truncations at Romans 2:15 'them', Romans 2:15 'bears witness' (closing text) and Romans 3:23 are fair. The closing texts use the *"Quote."* (Reference) form.

Scripture paraphrases are accurate against the ESV copy: Mark 10:17 (ran up, knelt), 10:19-22, 10:26; Romans 1 idolatry and cruelty (1:23, 29-31); and 'Mark adds a detail the other Gospels leave out' (Matthew 19:16-22 and Luke 18:18-23 lack 'loved him'). The heading's 'young' is from Matthew 19:20.

Myers quotation 'how inconceivable was the first, how unbelievable the second, and yet how peremptory and absolute the third.' is verbatim in Cooke (PG 11680) and Morley (PG 17954), both re-read today; only the italics are dropped. 'Took three words as her text, God, Immortality and Duty', 'Fellows' Garden of Trinity' and 'rainy May' come from the same passage. May 1873 rests on Eliot's journal in Cross (ledger).

Locke quotation is verbatim in modern spelling. Re-read today against the 1689 first edition (TCP A48884: 'Lastly, Those are not at all to be tolerated who deny the Being of a God. Promises, Covenants, and Oaths, which are the Bonds of Humane Society, can have no hold upon an Atheist. The taking away of God, tho but even in thought, dissolves all.') and the 1743 Boston reprint (N04240, 'though'). The essay's closing period matches 1689. The period after 'a God' becomes a comma at the dialogue tag, which is standard. 'Published in English in 1689' is verified.

Justin, First Apology 6, re-read today in ANF: 'Hence are we called atheists. And we confess that we are atheists, so far as gods of this sort are concerned, but not with respect to the most true God, the Father of righteousness and temperance and the other virtues' is verbatim. The period becomes a comma at the tag, and the quotation is truncated before ', who is free from all impurity'. Chapter 4 (judged by the name, not the deeds) supports the paraphrase. Antoninus Pius and 'in the 150s' rest on ledger correction 3 of the restoration pass.

Martyrdom of Polycarp, re-read today in ANF. Chapter 3 has the crowd's cry 'Away with the Atheists; let Polycarp be sought out!'. Chapter 9 has the proconsul's 'Swear by the fortune of Caesar; repent, and say, Away with the Atheists', then Polycarp's stern look, wave of the hand, groans, look to heaven, and 'Away with the Atheists.' The essay's sequence and capitalization match. 'Middle of that century' is kept general and is supported.

Pew, confirmed today on pewresearch.org (Gregory A. Smith, October 16, 2017, short read): 56 percent in 2017, up from 49 percent in 2011; white evangelical Protestants 26 to 32 percent; the share saying belief is necessary fell from 72 to 65 percent, which supports 'most of them still said belief in God was necessary'.

Gervais, confirmed today. The pure.royalholloway.ac.uk and researchonline.jcu.edu.au abstracts give Nature Human Behaviour 2017, N = 3,256 in 13 countries, with prejudice evident even among atheist participants. Press coverage (lifestyle.inquirer.net, cbn.com, hinduismtoday.com) describes the vignette as a man who tortured animals as a child and later killed five homeless people, and reports people roughly twice as likely to see extreme immorality as representative of atheists. The essay paraphrases the vignette and uses no quotation marks.

Nietzsche: today's exact-phrase search matched 'They are rid of the Christian God and now believe all the more firmly that they must cling to Christian morality' on reformedperspective.ca, salvomag.com and johnheersftf.substack.com. The second sentence rests on the restoration pass's exact-phrase matches. Both render the German of Streifzuege 5 (ledger). The essay does not name a translator. The Kaufmann book itself was not seen by any run, but the wording is consistent across independent copies, so the quotation marks can stay. Twilight of the Idols naming G. Eliot is verified, as are the single-system paraphrase and the inheritance paraphrase.

Mackie (Australian-born, at Oxford, error theorist; Ethics: Inventing Right and Wrong 1977; argument from queerness; The Miracle of Theism 1982, after his death in December 1981; the concession given as unquoted paraphrase), Street (2006 paper; the coincidence sentence as corrected; antirealist conclusion), Wielenberg (atheist; necessary, foundationless basic ethical facts; 'as Wielenberg himself argues'): all match their ledger lines and the ledger's corrections. Wielenberg's last-paragraph sentence is the one exception (finding 2).

Euthyphro (399 BC, King Archon's porch, father prosecuted over the death of a hired man, Socrates' question), Aquinas (ST I q.6 a.3-4), Bayle in 1680s Rotterdam (virtuous atheist, society of atheists; EB1911, Voltaire, Robertson), and Eliot's biography (evangelical girlhood, left the faith at about 22, Strauss translation published 1846, Middlemarch's last book December 1872): all match ledger lines.
Biography: the only biographical line is 'I was an atheist before I was a Christian', which NOTES.md confirms. No title, years, book count or denomination is given.
Second-order questions: how much of the evolutionary history to accept is named as a question Christians differ on and left open. James's position is not asserted.
Living persons (f): Gervais and Street are described fairly. Wielenberg is described fairly ('take right and wrong at least as seriously as most Christians do') except for the sentence in finding 2.

Mechanics in the published body: 0 em-dashes, 0 exclamation points, 0 double hyphens, and no word from the CLAUDE.md forbidden list. The two links, /writing/the-early-church-under-rome and /writing/why-didnt-the-bible-ban-slavery, both have published JSON in client/public/essays, so they resolve to public essays. The dropped link to the-children-rome-threw-away (not on the shelf) was correctly removed, but see finding 1.
Published JSON against the ledger's markdown (docs/work/essays/can-you-be-good-without-god.md): the only text difference is the removed children link.
